     By a (pure) automaton, we will mean a 3-sorted algebra ~ = (As G, B), where A Is a set
of states, G a semigroup of input signals and B a set of output signals, i.eo~ external s
states, and we assume that the automaton comes with a transition operation~ o: A x G + A,
and an output operation, ,: A x G § B, bound by the conditions a,og~g.~=(aogl) og2, a ~ g ~ g ~ =
(aog0~g2.  If A and B are modules over some ring K, and the operations o and * are linear,
then ~I is called a linear automaton.     An automaton @I is called a Mur automaton if there is
a map I:A § B such that a , g = (a ~ g)~.   It is easy to show that 9~ is a pure Mur automaton
if, and only if, the quasi-identity X~oy~=x2oy2~ z~y=----x2~y2 holds, and a linear a u t o m a t o n ~
is a Mur automaton if, and only if, p is a linear map, and the quasi-identity


                                      i=l           i=l

is valid, where    x~A~   ~G,   and the u i are elements of the free semigroup algebra KG I.
     These and many other considerations      make it necessary   to construct a general theory of
quasivarieties of automata.
     Higgins [I] gave an invariant characteristic of varieties of many-sorted algebras (cf.
[2] for its application to automata).  The corresponding characteristic of quasivarieties,
that generalizes Mal'tsev's well-known theorem [3], can be found in [4]: A class of many-
sorted algebras is a quasivariety if, and only if, it is closed relative to filtered prod-
ucts, is hereditary and contains the identity algebra.  In our paper, this characteristic is
applied to automata.
     Our paper consists of three sections.  The first two are devoted to quasivarieties of
automata.  We define classes of automata, saturated relative to input and output signals.
These are dual concepts.
         In Sec. I, we concern ourselves with questions about saturation relative to input sig-
nals, and in Sec. 2, saturation relative to output signals.        It is shown that saturation
relative to input signals is equivalent to the quasivariety being presentable by quasi-iden-
ties that do not involve any equations relating to the semigroup.        On the other hand, quasi-
varieties of pure automata, as well as of automata linear over a field, are saturated rela-
tive to output signals if, and only if, it is possible to exclude from their defining quasi-
identities all variables over the set of output signals.       Moreover, if ~   is a quasivariety
of automata, saturated relative to input signals, and G is a semigroup, then we will let ~G
denote the fiber consisting of all automata (J, G, B ) ~ .      Each of these G-automata can be
viewed as a 2-sorted algebra, the elements of G being considered as operations.         The fiber
is also a quasivariety.      We give a determination, in terms of fibers, of quasivarieties sat-
urated relative to input signals.       This determination serves as the basis for the character-
istic, mentioned above, of quasi varieties saturated with respect to input signals.        We con-
sider connections between quasivarieties of automata, saturated with respect to input sig-
n a l s , and quasivarieties of semigroups.   To each quasivariety of automata $, saturated rela-
tive to input signals, there corresponds a quasivariety of semigroups $, consisting of all
semigroups that admit ~ faithful representation in $.        It is shown that this correspondance
is surjective.      A series of results, contained in the first two sections, generalize the cor-
responding results in [5].
     Section 3 is devoted to an application of the methods of many-sorted algebras to the
theory of quasigroups.  This application is founded upon the concept of reversible automaton,
viz., a triple (A, B, C) of sets of the same cardinality, with only one operation ,: A x B +
C, invertible on both sides.  So, a reversible automaton is a 3-sorted quasigroup [6]. What
we have in mind here is the reversibility of the automaton relative to the output function,
        Translated from Sibirskii Matematicheskii Zhurnal,   Vol. 26, No. 3, pp.   71-30, May-June,
!985.     Original article submitted November 16, 7983.


               0037-4466/85/2603-0315509.50     9 1986 Plenum Publishing   Corporation              3!5
as distinct from reversibility relative to the transition function, as considered in [7]~
Every quasigroup Q can be considered as a regular reversible automaton (Q, Q, Q). Two quasi-
groups Q and Q' are isotopic if, and only if, their corresponding regular reversible auto-
mata are isomorphic.  This approach allows one to prove, for instance, the following propo-
sitions: If @ is some variety (reap., quasivariety) of groups, then the class of all quasi-
groups, isotopic to groups in @, is also a variety (reap., quasivariety) (a generalization
of the corresponding results in [8, 9]); every reversible automaton (A, B, C) is isomorphic
to some regular automaton (Q, Q, Q), where Q is a loop (as a consequence of this proposition,
we have the well-known fact that every quasigroup is LP-isotopic to some loop [6], and the
proposition reveals the real reason why this is so). We also give some other results about
reversible automata.

            1.   QUASIVARIETIES       OF AUTOMATA,   SATURATED RELATIVE TO INPUT SIGNALS
     Let  ~ = (A, G, B) be a semigroup automaton, SA the semigroup of all permutations of the
set A, Fun (A, B) the set of all mappings from A into B and S(A, B) = SA • Fun (A, B). By de-
fining on S(A, B) the following operation


we obtain a semigroup.
      If ~ is a linear automaton, i.e., A and B are modules over some associative, commutative
ring K with identity, then we have to replace S(A, B) above by the semigroup E(A, B) = E n d A •
Hom (A, B), endowed with the analogous operation of multiplication.
     The operations o and , define a homomorphism ~:G § S(A, B) of pure automata and a homo-
morphism ~:@ § E(A, B) of linear automata.   The kernel equivalence of this homomorphism is
called the kernel of the automaton ~.    An automaton with trivial kernel is called faithful.
     Unless we indicate otherwise, the term automaton will mean a linear semigroup automaton
over some associative, commutative ring K with identity.  However, the results below are also
true for pure automata, as well as for group and ring automata.
     Definition.  A class ~ of automata is said to be saturated relative to inputs if for
every epimorphism (A, GI, B) * (A, G2, B) on inputs, the following holds: (A, GI, B ) ~ < ~ ( A , Gz,
B ) ~ ~.

     Let (A, G, ~) be a given automaton.  Every element g ~ G defines two operations: g~   §
A and g*:A § B. For fixed semigroup G of input signals, the automaton can be considered as
a 2-sorted system (A, B), the elements of G being viewed as operations.  The associated pair
(A, B) will be called a G-automaton. If ~ now denotes a class of automata and G is a semi-
group, then we will let ~   denote the class of G-automata (A, B) for which (A, G, B ) ~ (the
fiber of G-automata from ~).

~   of an hereditary class ~, saturated relative to inputs, is a quasivariety, then ~ is
likewise a quasivariety.

longs to ~ , i.e., each class ~G is non-empty and contains an identity object.

                                  2.   SATURATION RELATIVE TO OUTPUT SIGNALS
     Definition.  A class $ of automata is called saturated relative to output signals, if
the following condition holds: let (A, G, B) be some automaton and (A, G, B0) some subauto-
maton with the same A and G. The class ~ is saturated relative to output signals if always
                                             (A, G, B ) ~ ~ = ~ ( A ,       G, B 0 ) ~ ~.
We will introduce yet another operator V1: V ~ consists of those automata                                (A, G, B) that
admit a subautomaton (A, G, B0) belonging to the class ~.
     One can verify that the smallest quasivariety of automata,                             saturated relative              to output
signals and generated by some class ~, is the class V'SC'~.
     We will relate the condition of saturation relative to output signals to the exclusion
from the quasi-identities of variables from the set Z [we remind the reader that (X, Y, Z)
is a system of free generators for the free automaton W].
     Proposition I. If the variables in Z are absent from the quasi-identities that define
a quasivariety X of automata, then the quasivariety is saturated relative to output signals.
      Proof.   Suppose that ~. is defined by quasi-identities without variables from Z, let
(A, G, B) be some automaton with subautomaton (A, G~ B0) belonging to ~.     We will show that
(A~ G, ~ ) ~ .  To this end, we have to verify that every quasi-identity


without variables from Z, and appearing in a presentation for the class ~, is also valid in
(A, G, B).  Suppose that we are given a homomorphism ~ : W §             G, B), and suppose that the
following equations hold in (A, G, B): u ~ = u ~ A u ~ = u ~ h ... A u ~ = v ~ . Since the variables in
Z are absent from the u i and vi, these last equations are already valid in the subautomaton
(A, G, B0).  Since the latter lies in ~, we also have u[+ 1 = v~+ !.
     A free object in the category of pure automata                          is of the form W = (X oF ~, F~ X { F O Z ) ,
where F = F(Y), and X, Y, Z are countable sets.

     We now come to the following general problem: In which cases can a quasivariety of auto-
mata ~ be defined b y a collection of quasi-identities that splits into two groups, with one con-
taining quasi-identities that do not admit any variables from Z, and the other consisting of
quasi-identities that are written entirely in variables from Z?
      In essence, the second group will determine quasivarieties of modules of output signals,
whereas the first would only define quasivarieties of automata that are saturated relative to
output signals.
     We saw, in the case of a field, that every quasivariety       of automata,   saturated relative
to output signals, has this property.
     We observe that the concepts relating to automata being saturated relative to input and
output signals can be carried over to arbitrary many-sorted algebras.

                                    3.    REVERSIBLE AUTOMATA
      In this section, we will consider automata (A, B, C) with a single operation of outputs
*: A • B § C, where A, B, and C are, respectively, the sets of states, of input signals and
of output signals.    For these automatic, the concepts of subautomaton, homomorphism~
Cartesian product, etc., are defined in the usual manner.    The indicated automaton is said
to be reversible if, in the equation a * b = c every pair of elements uniquely determines the
third, i.e., knowing an output signal and a state, the given input signal is uniquely deter-
mined; also, knowing the input and output signals, the state can be uniquely established.
     It is obvious that the Cartesian product of reversible automata is again a reversible
automaton.  However, a subautomaton of a reversible automaton need not be reversible~ for
instance, the triple (A, b, C), where b ~ B ,  is a subautomaton of the reversible automaton
(A, B, C), but it is not reversible.   It is easily seen that in a reversible automaton the
sets A, B, and C must be of equal cardinality.    The homomorphic image of a reversible auto-
maton is not necessarily reversible.   For instance, let (A, B, C) be a reversible automaton
and ~3:C § C' any map.   We define an automaton (A, B, C') by putting a * b = ( a , b ) ~3, where
the * in brackets refers to the original reversible automaton.    The resulting automaton (A,
B, C') is the homomorphic image of (A, B, C). The set C' can be taken to consist of a single
element, and (A, B, C') will then not always be reversible.
     It is appropriate, in view of the above, to consider a reversible automaton as a struc-
ture with three operations, viz., the operation , and its two inverses / and \, where a * b =
c~=~a\c=b~=~c/b=a . In addition, the following identities hold for arbitrary elements a ~ A ,
b~B, and c ~ C :
                                    a,(a\c)=c;       (c/b),b=c,
                                    a\(a,b)=b,       (a,b)/b=a.
If the three sets A, B, and C coincide, then this defines at the same time the structure of
a quasigroup.  A reversible automaton is a quasigroup split into three parts, i.e., a 3-
sorted quasigroup.
      If, on the other hand, Q is some quasigroup, then there is a corresponding regular re-
versible automaton (Q, Q, Q).   In addition, a homotopy (resp., isotopy) of quasigroups Q § QV
is nothing else than a homomorphism (resp., isomorphism) of the corresponding regular auto-
mata.
     The theory of reversible automata is close to the theory of quasigroups, however it is
important to make the distinction.    If, for instance, a and b are arbitrary elements in A
and B, respectively, and c = a ' b , then the triple (a, b, c) is a reversible subautomaton in
(A, B, C), with singleton underlying sets.    Every such subautomaton of a reversible automaton
will be called an identity reversible automaton.


326
     The concept of reversible automaton has applications, not only in the theory of auto-
mata, but also in the theory of quasigroups.  We will consider some of these applications in
this section.
     Let Q(*) be an arbitrary quasi-group, A, B, and C three of its subsets, having the fol-
lowing property: if we have an equation a * b = c, then
        1)   a~A     and b ~ B      imply c ~ C ,
       2)    a~A     and    c~C     imply b ~ B ,
       3)     b~,,B and     c~C     imply a ~ A .
In this case, the triple (A, B, C) can be considered as a reversible automaton.                                                Such an auto-
maton will be called an automaton in the q~asi-group Q(*).
     If ~ = (~, ~, y) is a homotopy of the quasigreup Q into a quasigroup Q', preserving all
three quasigroup operations, then (Qa, Q$, QY) is obviously an automaton in the quasigroup Q'
     One can consider, in particular, automata in groups.   Let G be a group, H a subgroup,
and x, y ~ G . Then the triple (Hx, x-iHxy, Hxy) is an automaton in the group G:

                                                         h~x 9x-~h~xy = hllhxy ~ Hxy,

Moreover, every such automaton is isomorphic to the regular automaton (H, H, H)~ the isomor-
phism ~ = (Pl, V2, ~3) being defined by h vx = hx, h ~2 = x-lhxy, h v3 = hxy: if hih2 = h3 then

     THEOREM 7. If (A, B, C) is an automaton in a group G('), then there exist a subgroup
H~G    and elements z, N ~ G such that A = Hx, B = x-iHxy, C = Hxy and the automaton coincides
with the automaton defined by the subgroup H and the elements x, y.
     Proof.     First, we will show that if all three sets A, B, and C contain the identity

     We have shown above that the automaton (Ha, a-~Hab, Hab) is isomorphic to the regular auto-

     Besides the concept of an automaton in a quasigroup, we will also consider quotient auto-
mata of quasigroups.  Let Q(*) be a quasigroup and Pz, 02, p3 three equivalence relations on
the set Q, such that, given two equations a * b = c and a' *b' = c', we have
        )    aPlW A bP~b~=>'cp~c',
       2)    apla' A epic' =~ bp~b',
       3)    bp~b' A epic' =>.ap~a'..
       Such a triple of equivalence relations will be called an automaton equivalence in the
quasigroup.
      Under these conditions, the triple of sets (Q/pl, Q/02, Q/p~) define a reversible auto-
maton, which is a quotient of Q(*).   The basic operation of this automaton is defined by the
equa t ion

The inverses of this operation are also defined                    in the corresponding      manner.
     Proposition 2. If p = (Pl, P2, p3) is an automaton equivalence                            in a loop Q(*), then
pz = P2 = p3 = P is a loop congruence of Q(*).
       Proof. Let bp2b'    Then b = ebp3eb' = b', where e is the identity element of Q(*), and
hence p2 ~p3. Conversely, if cp3c' then the equations c = ec, c' = ec' imply cp2c', i.e.,
P3 ~p2, and hence 02 = P3.   One can verify in an analogous manner that pz = p3, and it then
follows from the definition of an automaton equivalence that p is a loop congruence of Q(*).
     From Proposition 2 follows, in particular, that if G is a group, then each of its quo-
tient automata is a regular automaton of the form (G/H, G/H, G/H), where H is a normal sub-
group of G.
      We will apply the above concepts              to prove the following theorem.
     THEOREM 8. Let @ be some variety of groups and let ~ denote the class of quasigroups
isotopic to groups in O. Then O is a variety of quasigroups.
     Proof.   Let Q ~ O ,  and let Q1 be a subquasigroup of Q. We will show that Q ~ O .    By
hypothesis, there is an isotopy p = (~, B, y) of a quasigroup Q with a group G ~ O .     We con-
sider the three sets (QI, Qz, Qz ) in G.    Since QI is a subquasigroup and ~ defines an iso-
morphism of the regular automaton (Qz, Qz, Ql) with (Q~, Q~, Q~), it follows that the latter
triple is an automaton in the group G. By the above, the latter is isomorphic to some regular
automaton (H, H, H), where H is a subgroup of G. Hence, the automata (Qz, Qz, QI) and
(H, H, H) are isomorphic, and the quasigroup Ql is therefore isotopic to the group H. But,
since H ~ O , we have Q I ~ O .
     If p is a congruence on the quasigroup Q ~ ,   then the quotient quasigroup Q/p belongs
to O.    Indeed, we have by assumption an isotopy ~ = (~, ~, ? ) : Q - ~ G ~ . Hence, we have an
isomorphism of automata (Q, Q, Q) and (G, G, G). We will consider the corresponding images
of the congruence p, i.e., (p~, pB, pY).   This is an automaton equivalence in the group G,
and we have an isomorphism of the automata (Q/p, Q/p, Q/p) and (G/p ~, G/p B, G/pY).     As we
already observed, pa, pB, and pY coincide among each other, and define a normal subgroup H
of G. The automaton (Q/p, Q/p, Q/p) is then isomorphic to the regular automaton (G/H, G/H,
G/H), from which it follows that the quasigroup Q/p is isotopic to the group G / H ~ O , and,
consequently, Q / p ~ O .
      We now take a collection of quasigroups Q~, i~I, belonging to the class O.    For each

     A class of quasigroups that is closed under arbitrary isotopies will be called ~ g v e r s a ~ .

     Remarks.  ~) The above results show that the variety of all reversible automata contains
quite a lot of subvarieties and subquasivarieties.
       2) It is easily seen that if two varieties                                       (reap., quasivarieties)         of groups     @~    and @2
are distinct, then the varieties (reap., quasivarieties)   O~ and O2 of automata are likewise
distinct.   Indeed, let G be a group belonging to O~ but not to 02. Then the regular auto-
maton (G, G, G) belongs to O~. Suppose that (G, G, G) also belongs to O2. By hypothesis,
we can then find a group H in 02, such that the regular automata (G, G, G) and (H, H, H) are
isomorphic.   This means that the groups G and H are isotopic, but it is well known that G and
H must then also be isomorphic.   So, G lies in @2, which contradicts the hypothesis.   We see
at the same time that different varieties (reap., quasivarieties) of groups correspond to dif-
ferent varieties (reap., quasivarieties) of quasigr.oups.
     3) One can enrich the structure of a reversible automaton by supposing that the set of
input signals B is a quasigroup, and that we are given a representation of this quasigroup
on the set A of states.  In addition, this representation must be assumed to be connected to
the corresponding operation *.

      Remark Inserted in Proof.  The author has proved at this point that, over an arbitrary
ring, the condition of a quasivariety being saturated relative to output signals is equiva-
lent to its being defined by quasi-identities that do not involve any output variables.   How-
ever, the hereditary property of being finitely based, contained in Theorems 5 and 6, may
fail.   As a consequence of this result, the problem mentioned on p.326 has been solved.

STRONG LINEAR CONVEXITY.
I.   DUALITY OF SPACES OF HOLOMORPHIC FUNCTIONS

      S~ V. Znamenskii                                                                        UDC 5~7.55


                                            INTRODUCTION
      I~ Let /~ be an open set in C. The space H(.~) consists of functions w~ich are holo -o
morphic in /~, and convergence in H(/~) by definition means uniform convergence on each com-
pact subset of 6_~.
     Let 6 ~ be an arbitrary set in C. We define the space H(3-) as the inductive limit of
the spaces H(/~) over all open /~ containing ~ .      The space H0(6~) is defined as the closed
subspace of H(6~), consisting of functions which vanish at infinity if ~ - c C ,     and is iden-
tified with H ( ~ ) if 6 ~ c C . By H~(~') we denote the space of continuous linear functionals
on H0(~-). For each T ~ H ~ (~-) , the formula

                                         9 ~(~) = T((~_      Z)-~)                                        (~)
defines a function   ~H0(C\6~),   the indicatrix of this functional;
     The basic result (cf. [~, 2]) of the theory of duality of spaces of holomorphic functions
developed in [3-5] asserts that for a set /~- from a certain class which includes all open
and all_compact sets in C, the correspondence (I) establishes an isomorphism of spaces H~(F)
and H0(C\6~). Examples of the use of this theorem to prove Runge~s theorem, the theorems on
interpolation and ideals, and the theorem of Poincare--Aronszaijn on the separation of singu-
larities are given in [2, 6].
     Considering multidimensional analogs of the duality theorem, we shall assume that /~
is holomorphically nonextendable, i.e., for each z ~ 6 ~ there exists an /~H(6~), which can-
not be extended analytically to the point z. We also require that 6~ be open or a compact
set.  These requirements on ~ will be understood in the formulations of all assertions of
the paper.
